ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Written informed consent was obtained before any study procedures, which were performed in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration and Good Clinical Practice (GCP).

> Thirty-five men and women aged 20-65 years and meeting the ICD-10 criteria of an episode of recurrent moderate to severe MDD (Montgomery Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) >22 points) were recruited through advertising on social media platforms (Table 1) (32).

> Participants were required to remain free of depression treatment throughout the first six weeks of follow-up.

> Participants were randomized 1:1 to a single dose of 25mg psilocybin or 100mg niacin placebo, both treatment arms received five sessions of psychotherapeutic support from day -1 to day 15.

> The first 26 participants were scanned on a 3-Tesla General Electric Discovery MR750 scanner, and the remaining 9 on a 3-Tesla GE SIGNA Premier scanner.

> During scanning, participants were positioned supine, with the head fixated.

> Four participants had translational displacement > 4 mm in at least one scan, for which motion correction was performed by frame-wise coregistration to the corresponding transmission image and retained if it resulted in changes > 5% in regional outcome estimates and applied to the corresponding paired scan as well.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

Thirty-five men and women aged 20-65 years and meeting the ICD-10 criteria of an episode of recurrent moderate to severe MDD (Montgomery Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) >22 points) were recruited through advertising on social media platforms (Table 1) (32).
Participants were required to remain free of depression treatment throughout the first six weeks of follow-up.
Participants were randomized 1:1 to a single dose of 25mg psilocybin or 100mg niacin placebo, both treatment arms received five sessions of psychotherapeutic support from day -1 to day 15.
The first 26 participants were scanned on a 3-Tesla General Electric Discovery MR750 scanner, and the remaining 9 on a 3-Tesla GE SIGNA Premier scanner.
During scanning, participants were positioned supine, with the head fixated.

Four participants had translational displacement > 4 mm in at least one scan, for which motion correction was performed by frame-wise coregistration to the corresponding transmission image and retained if it resulted in changes > 5% in regional outcome estimates and applied to the corresponding paired scan as well.

text.text: We report a pre-registered [ 11 C]UCB-J PET sub-study of a recently published randomized trial in which a single psilocybin dose produced rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in major depressive disorder (MDD).

Synaptic loss has been implicated in MDD, and psychedelics induce synaptic remodeling in preclinical models within 24 hours, raising the possibility that psilocybin's antidepressant effects involve increased synaptic density.

We used the PET radioligand [ 11 C]UCB-J targeting synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) to test this in thirty-five participants with moderate-to-severe recurrent MDD randomized 1:1 to a single dose of 25 mg psilocybin or 100 mg niacin placebo, both with psychotherapeutic support.
[ 11 C]UCB-J PET was performed 2-7 days before and 15 (±7) days after dosing.
Despite significant clinical improvement in the psilocybin group, we found no evidence of a group-level increase in SV2A binding (VT or BPND) relative to niacin in the hippocampus or frontal cortex.

In secondary analyses, higher baseline VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in the psilocybin group; this survived FDR correction at Day 8 and Day 15 (two of three pre-registered timepoints).

Change in VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in unadjusted analyses, but these associations were attenuated after adjustment for baseline VT and baseline MADRS and did not survive FDR correction.

These findings indicate that substantial antidepressant improvement after psilocybin can occur without a detectable group-level increase in SV2A binding, while raising the possibility that baseline SV2A binding could help identify individuals more likely to respond.

Synaptic plasticity contributes to resilience and adaptation throughout life (1-5), whereas synaptic dysfunction has been implicated in a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions (6) (7) (8), including major depressive disorder (MDD).

text.text: There is ongoing debate regarding how synaptic alterations in depression are to be interpreted.
One simplified "loss-restoration" framework proposes that depression is associated with synaptic loss, whereas antidepressants can promote their restoration.

In contrast, perspectives such as iPlasticity suggest that treatment may induce a permissive state of heightened plasticity, in which environmental factors shape synaptic remodelling and clinical outcomes (22, 23).

text.text: Taken together, this debate leaves unresolved whether treatmentrelated plasticity manifests as an increase in synaptic density, and when such changes emerge in relation to treatment and clinical improvement.

The PET radioligand [ 11 C]UCB-J, targeting the synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), a presynaptic protein widely distributed throughout the brain, has shown close correspondence with the established synaptic marker synaptophysin, enabling estimation of synaptic density in the living human brain (24) (25) (26).

Against this background, we examined [ 11 C]UCB-J PET data from a recently published randomized clinical trial in which psilocybin produced rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in patients with MDD (32).

text.text: A bolus injection containing approximately 400 MBq (±10%, for a participant of 70 kg) was injected via antecubital venous cannula, followed by a saline flush.
A 6-min transmission scan using a rotating ¹³⁷Cs source was acquired for attenuation correction, followed by a 90-min emission scan acquired in list mode.

Dynamic images were reconstructed into 37 frames (8 × 15 s, 8 × 30 s, 4 × 60 s, 5 × 120 s, 10 × 300 s, 2 × 600 s) using OP-3D-OSEM with point spread function modelling, yielding a resolution of approximately 2 mm at the center of the field of view.
Arterial blood was sampled via a radial artery cannula for derivation of the arterial input function (AIF) and radiometabolite correction.
Continuous sampling was performed during the first 10 minutes using an Automatic Blood Sampling System (ABSS, Alogg technologies, Mariefred, Sweden) followed by discrete manual samples.
The parent fraction in plasma and its radiometabolite profile were determined using protein precipitation followed by reversed-phase radio-HPLC.
Head motion was estimated using realignment of all frames to a reference formed from the first frames (first 4 min) in SPM.

Four participants had translational displacement > 4 mm in at least one scan, for which motion correction was performed by frame-wise coregistration to the corresponding transmission image and retained if it resulted in changes > 5% in regional outcome estimates and applied to the corresponding paired scan as well.

text.text: All image processing and kinetic modelling were conducted blinded to treatment allocation, using randomized study identifiers.
Depressive symptoms were assessed using the MADRS, by blinded raters.
Assessments were performed at baseline (PET1), follow-up PET (PET2), and on days 8, 42, and 365 post-dose.
Acute subjective drug effects were assessed using the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ-30) and the Scale for Psychedelic Intensity Rating (SPIR).
SPIR ratings were obtained approximately 90 minutes after dosing, while MEQ-30 was administered at the end of the dosing session.
Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ) and Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (EBI) were used to assess challenging psychological reactions to psychedelics.
They were administered at the end of the dosing session.
The Lasting Effects Questionnaire (LEQ) is a fusion of questions from CEQ, MEQ and EBI, measuring lasting effects of psychedelic experience, administered at day 8, 15, 42 and 365.
Psychological flexibility was assessed using the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II (AAQ-II).
AAQ-II was administered during treatment sessions and at follow-up assessments at days 42 and 365.

The Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) and Meaning in Life Questionnaire (MLQ) assessed subjective well-being and meaning in life, respectively, and were administered during treatment sessions and at Days 42 and 365.

text.text: The dependent variable was [ 11 C]UCB-J binding, and the primary regions of interest (ROIs) were the bilateral hippocampus (HIP) and frontal cortex (FC).
For each outcome measure (i.e.
VT and BPND) and ROI we fitted an ANCOVA model with PET2 as the dependent variable, treatment group as predictor and the corresponding PET1 value as covariate.
Both VT and BPND were preregistered outcome measures.

VT was emphasized because it is estimated using an arterial input function and does not rely on a reference region, thereby avoiding assumptions regarding stability of the centrum semiovale across treatment conditions; BPND was reported as a complementary reference-tissue measure.
Analyses were conducted in three steps.

In Model 1 we adjusted for PET1 only; in Model 2 we additionally included time from dosing to PET2 (days); and in Model 3 we further adjusted for age and clinical covariates (duration of current episode, baseline depression severity, and number of previous episodes).
The significance level was set to 0.05.
Given the high interregional correlations for the binding outcomes, no correction for multiple testing was applied.
Outlier detection, quality control and all analyses were conducted blinded to treatment allocation, using randomized study identifiers.
Secondary analyses examined whether change in [ 11 C]UCB-J binding from baseline to follow-up examination was associated with change in depressive symptom severity on the MADRS.

For the present PET sub study, the MADRS assessment obtained at the same visit as PET2 (Day 15 ±7) was prespecified as the primary clinical endpoint for analyses relating change in PET binding to clinical change.
Other follow-up assessments were days 8, 42 and 365.
For analyses involving MADRS outcomes at Day 42 and Day 365, observations obtained after post-randomization psychedelic use or reinitiation of antidepressant treatment were censored.
To account for multiple testing in the secondary analyses, false discovery rate (FDR) correction using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied within each analysis family.

For the preregistered correlation analyses, correction was performed separately within each treatment arm and clinical follow-up timepoint across the four regional binding measures (frontal cortex and hippocampus; VT and BPND).
For treatment-interaction analyses, FDR correction was applied across the eight interaction tests comprising two regions and four follow-up timepoints.

Additional post hoc analyses examining the ΔVT-ΔMADRS association after adjustment for baseline VT were treated as a separate analysis family, with FDR correction across the eight tests comprising two regions and four follow-up timepoints within each treatment arm.
Nominal and FDR-adjusted p values are reported throughout.
Pearson's correlation coefficients (r) were calculated between regional ΔVT (PET2 -PET1) and ΔMADRS (follow-up -baseline, negative values indicate improvement).
Parallel analyses for ΔBPND are reported in Supplementary Tables 2 3.

text.text: Analyses were conducted separately within each treatment arm.

To assess whether the association between ΔVT and ΔMADRS differed between treatment groups, we additionally fitted linear models with ΔMADRS as the dependent variable and ΔVT, treatment, and ΔVT × treatment as independent variables.
The interaction term was interpreted as the formal test of between-group difference in associations.

Because baseline VT was itself associated with clinical outcome and is mathematically incorporated in Δ VT, we performed additional post hoc analyses to assess whether the ΔVT-ΔMADRS association was independent of baseline binding.
Partial Pearson correlations between ΔVT and ΔMADRS were calculated controlling for baseline VT.
We additionally fitted linear models including baseline MADRS, baseline VT, and ΔVT as predictors of ΔMADRS.
Variance inflation factors were examined to assess collinearity between baseline VT and ΔVT.
These analyses were considered exploratory robustness analyses.

Fully interacted models, including treatment interactions with baseline MADRS, baseline VT, and ΔVT, were additionally fitted to assess whether the adjusted ΔVT-ΔMADRS association differed between treatment groups.
We also examined whether baseline [ 11 C]UCB-J binding was associated with antidepressant response on the same timepoints.
Pearson's correlations were calculated between baseline regional binding and ΔMADRS in both treatment arms.
In addition, linear models including baseline binding, treatment, and their interaction were fitted to test whether these associations differed between groups.
For baseline VT × treatment interaction analyses, FDR correction was applied across the eight tests comprising two regions and four follow-up timepoints.
Post hoc ROC analyses were performed in the psilocybin group using the response criterion specified in the statistical analysis plan (≥50% reduction in MADRS or >10-point reduction from baseline).

text.text: AUC estimates and 95% confidence intervals were obtained using stratified bootstrap resampling (10,000 iterations).
As a post hoc robustness analysis, associations between baseline VT and ΔMADRS were additionally adjusted for baseline MADRS to assess whether they were independent of initial depression severity.

Exploratory Spearman rank correlations were conducted to examine associations between regional ΔVT and ΔBPND and psychological outcome measures, including MEQ total score and subscales, SPIR, CEQ, EBI, as well as change in AAQ-II, LEQ, MLQ and SWLS at the available follow-up timepoints.

Finally, we repeated the same ANCOVA model used in the primary analysis across an extended set of anatomically defined ROIs that have previously been implicated in the neurobiology of MDD, including the anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortices, insula, amygdala, thalamus, and striatal regions, as well as global grey matter.

text.text: In this placebo-controlled experiment in patients with MDD, we found no evidence that a single 25 mg dose of psilocybin administered with psychotherapeutic support increased synaptic density, indexed by [ 11 C]UCB-J binding to SV2A, two weeks after administration, despite rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in the psilocybin group.
However, confidence intervals were wide and small-to-moderate treatment effects cannot be excluded.

This finding contrasts with a report of increased SV2A binding following psilocybin administration in the pig brain (28), but is consistent with a recent study in healthy volunteers that found no significant overall increase in SV2A binding one week after psilocybin, underscoring that translation to humans remains uncertain (40).
text.formatted: This finding contrasts with a report of increased SV2A binding following psilocybin administration in the pig brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>, but is consistent with a recent study in healthy volunteers that found no significant overall increase in SV2A binding one week after psilocybin, underscoring that translation to humans remains uncertain <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref>.

text.text: Our finding extends this observation to patients with MDD, providing no support for a simple synaptic lossrestoration model of psilocybin's antidepressant effects.

While SV2A PET may not capture all treatment-related synaptic plasticity, the findings are also consistent with the possibility that the antidepressant effects are mediated through other pathways, including expectancy and unblinding effects.

In the secondary analyses, higher baseline SV2A binding was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in the psilocybin group, with associations surviving correction for multiple comparisons at Day 8 and PET2 in both regions examined.
Associations remained in the same direction at Day 42 and Day 365 but did not survive FDR correction.

One possible interpretation is that higher SV2A binding reflects a greater synaptic reserve that may facilitate treatment response, even if the antidepressant effect itself is not accompanied by an increase in SV2A binding.

This finding raises the possibility that SV2A binding is associated with treatment response, but because the treatment interactions did not survive FDR correction it cannot be determined whether this reflects a psilocybin-specific predictor or a general prognostic marker.
The ability to identify patients likely to respond could improve the risk-benefit balance of psilocybin treatment as it moves toward clinical use.
In a post hoc analysis, we therefore explored its discriminative performance using receiver operating characteristic analyses.
At PET2, baseline VT showed good discrimination between responders and non-responders, with area under the curve values of 0.89 in frontal cortex and 0.91 in hippocampus.
These estimates should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample and the small number of non-responders and require prospective validation.

In contrast, the apparent association between greater reductions in VT and greater symptom improvement raised the possibility that psilocybin responders might show an early posttreatment reduction in SV2A binding.

This was contrary to our hypothesis, but given that SV2A expression seems to generally increase during brain maturation, this could hypothetically reflect transient synaptic remodeling during a period of heightened, juvenilelike plasticity (22, 41, 42).

text.text: However, this association was substantially attenuated after adjustment for baseline VT and baseline MADRS and did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
Fully adjusted interaction models provided no robust evidence that the association differed between treatment groups.
The study has several limitations, including the modest sample size.
Missing arterial data prevented estimation of VT for two participants in the psilocybin group.
The VT-MADRS analyses at Day 365 were based on a reduced sample due to censoring.
Plasma free fraction (fP) was not measured, limiting interpretation of VT.
As a presynaptic marker, SV2A binding may not capture postsynaptic or dendritic plasticity, such as spine remodeling, that could be relevant to treatment response.

In addition, the single follow-up PET scan at approximately 15 days provides only a limited temporal snapshot of post-treatment SV2A binding and could miss out on earlier transient or later changes arising downstream of the clinical response.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that psilocybin can exert antidepressant effects in MDD without detectable increases in SV2A binding compared to control, two weeks after treatment.
This does not rule out synaptic plasticity following psilocybin treatment but highlights the limitations of SV2A binding as a proxy marker.
Secondary findings raise the possibility that SV2A binding may have a predictive value for treatment response.
Put together, this suggests a more complex pattern than can be explained by a synaptic lossrestoration narrative.
Further clarification of the role of synaptic plasticity in psilocybin's antidepressant effects would benefit from larger samples, earlier and repeated PET assessments, and multimodal approaches.

Change from baseline to follow-up in VT and BPND in primary regions of interest by treatment group.

Associa ons between changes in regional [¹¹C]UCB-J binding and changes in depressive symptom severity across follow-up by treatment group.Associations between change in regional [¹¹C]UCB-J volume of distribution (ΔVₜ; PET2-PET1) and change in depressive symptom severity (ΔMADRS) in the psilocybin (blue) and niacin (red) groups.
Observations after antidepressant initiation or psychedelic use outside the study protocol were censored.
